e.t: This adjective describes something that has not been traveled over or cannot be passed through: “untrodden; impassable.” It can describe a route, ground, or way that people cannot use because no path has been made or passage is blocked. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Job, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Its exact force in any verse depends on what place or way the surrounding passage is describing.

Abiasaph is a personal name, rendered “Abiasaph” or “Aviasaf.” It identifies a person rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs five times, appearing once in Exodus and four times in 1 Chronicles. The available references preserve the name across genealogical and service-related lists, but the name itself does not provide a broader description of the person. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

This Greek LXX verb means to contend or fight, describing active struggle against opposition. It can refer to a determined effort in conflict rather than merely holding a disagreement. The word appears six times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach, 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains strenuous engagement or combat. The English renderings “fight” and “contend” reflect this basic meaning.

This word means “unlawfully,” describing an action done in violation of what is rightfully required or permitted. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea is conduct carried out against lawful or proper order.

This noun means “one who chooses”—a person characterized by making a choice or selection. It identifies the chooser rather than the choice itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 8:4. The word’s basic sense is therefore straightforward: someone who selects or decides between possibilities. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain what was chosen and what significance that choice has there.

This verb means “boil up; foam up,” describing something rising and bubbling until it froths. It expresses an active process rather than a settled condition: something swells, seethes, or breaks into foam. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 21:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning centers on vigorous boiling or foaming.

This Greek LXX verb means “move camp” or “move one’s camp.” It describes changing the location of a camp, emphasizing relocation rather than simply going somewhere. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 3:35. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself, but its basic meaning is the act of breaking camp and moving it elsewhere.

This Greek LXX verb means to “examine closely” or “investigate.” It describes careful, purposeful searching rather than a quick glance, expressing the act of looking into something in order to understand it. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 3:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is deliberate and thorough inquiry.

This adverb describes an action done in an unholy manner—that is, in a way contrary to what is holy or devoted to God. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Esther and once in 3 Maccabees, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here.

This verb describes being unfaithful or incredulous—that is, failing to remain loyal or refusing to believe. It presents unbelief or disloyalty as an action or condition, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in the deuterocanonical books: four times in Wisdom and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun describes repulsion—the feeling or act of being pushed away or rejected. It names a strong turning away from someone or something rather than simple distance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Lamentations 1:7, though the reference alone does not provide enough context to explain the word’s precise force in that verse. Its central meaning remains the experience or condition of repulsion, and the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on rejection, removal, or the resulting sense of abandonment.

Ariarathes, also rendered Ariarathis, is a proper name identifying a person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:22. Since this word is a personal name rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object, its central meaning is the individual’s name. The precise significance of that person in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Aroēdis is a proper name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is also represented by the name Arithis. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Genesis 46:16. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its identity and significance must be understood from that passage itself rather than from the name alone.

Asan is a proper name, rendered “Asan” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Joshua 19:7 and once in 1 Chronicles 6:44. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be identified here, but its lexical function is clear: Asan is a name used to designate someone or somewhere named in the biblical record.

Asernain, also rendered Asernen, is a proper name identifying a place or location in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general action, quality, or theological concept, but as a name used in the boundary descriptions of Numbers. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Numbers 34, at verses 9 and 10. Its exact geographic significance depends on the surrounding passage and the locations named there.

Assari is a proper name used as a distinctive designation, not a general term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in Joshua 19:37, so its lexical force is simply the identification of the named entity called Assari. The name itself does not provide an additional definition or description. Its precise referent and significance in that verse depend on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “curtain.” It refers to a hanging covering or divider, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle’s fabric furnishings. The word appears 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, with most occurrences in Exodus 26, where curtains are repeatedly specified. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a curtain used as a covering or partition. The precise role of a particular curtain depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “air in motion; breeze”—moving air, such as a natural current of wind. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, each in a different verse. Its ordinary meaning describes a physical movement of air rather than a person, object, or inward quality. The precise force of the word in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and its wording.

Bago, also given as “Vago,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Ezra 8:14. The available lexical information identifies it simply as the name Bago or Vago; it does not provide an expanded meaning or description. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This noun refers to an abomination—something regarded as deeply detestable or offensive. It names what is considered abhorrent rather than describing an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, the word occurs twice, in 1 Samuel 25:31 and Nahum 3:6. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a thing viewed with profound disgust or rejection.

Gaer is a proper name referring to a person named Gaer. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in Ezra 2:47. Because a personal name identifies someone rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept, its basic meaning is simply the person’s name. The surrounding verse would be needed to identify Gaer’s specific role or family connection there; the name itself does not provide those details.

Gelia, also rendered Yelia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in 1 Chronicles 4:18. The available meaning is limited to the name itself, so Scripture does not provide enough information here to assign it an additional definition or spiritual meaning. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

This noun means “murmuring; muttering”—spoken expressions of complaint or discontent. It names the act or sound of people speaking in a low, dissatisfied way rather than offering open, clear speech. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 14:27. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is murmuring or muttering. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

This Greek LXX noun refers to skill or cunning—the ability to carry out something with practiced competence or cleverness. Its basic sense can describe capable workmanship or clever ability, while the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is admirable skill or shrewd craft. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 2:13. The word itself names an ability, not a specific action or moral judgment; its precise force comes from how the sentence uses it.

This noun refers to a corrector or reformer—someone who sets something right or brings improvement. It describes a person associated with correction rather than merely stating that something is correct. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:15. The word’s central idea is therefore a person who rectifies, adjusts, or reforms what needs improvement, while the surrounding verse determines the specific application of that role.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “lie in ambush”: to remain hidden while waiting to attack or catch someone. It describes a deliberate, concealed position rather than ordinary sitting or waiting. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament, showing repeated use for hidden opposition or danger. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but the central idea remains staying concealed in readiness for an attack.

This Greek LXX verb means “step out of.” It describes movement from within something to outside it, functioning as an action word in a sentence. The basic idea is a person or thing coming out from a place or situation. It occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, so its central meaning remains consistent even when the surrounding passage determines what is being exited.

This noun means “extension”: something lengthened, stretched out, or reaching outward. It describes the idea of extending rather than naming a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 17:3. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its larger context, but its central sense remains the extending or lengthening of something.

This Greek word means “entangle”: to become caught, involved, or twisted together so that movement or separation is difficult. As a verb, it describes the action of entangling rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and how the entanglement is presented.

This verb means “support; rest upon,” describing something being placed on or relying upon something else. It expresses the action of leaning, resting, or being supported rather than standing independently. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:4. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly what is resting upon what, but the word itself centers on support and dependence.

This word describes inward thought—the private thinking or reflection taking place within a person. It points to what is held in the mind rather than something spoken or outwardly displayed. As an adjective, it characterizes something connected with inner thought. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 75:11; the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on internal thought.

This Greek LXX verb means “lead out; bring out,” describing the act of taking someone or something from one place and bringing it outward. It can refer to people, living creatures, or possessions being brought out, with the surrounding passage showing who acts and what is brought. The word occurs 213 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a broadly used action word rather than a rare expression.

This Greek LXX noun means “ruin” or “destruction”: the state of being brought to collapse or made desolate. It names a damaging outcome rather than an action, so it points to the result of devastation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Numbers and Jeremiah, making it an uncommon term. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

This Greek LXX verb means to admonish or charge someone. It describes a direct word of correction, warning, or firm instruction addressed to another person. The central idea is speaking with authority to restrain, correct, or call someone to account. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is an established but not frequent word there. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This noun means “interpretation”: the act or result of explaining the meaning of something so it can be understood. It points to making words, statements, or difficult matters clear rather than merely repeating them. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 47:17. The exact force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording, but its central sense remains interpretation.

This Greek LXX verb means to dye something with madder, making it red. It describes an action rather than simply naming the color, so it refers to the process of coloring a material red. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Exodus, where it is associated with materials used for the tabernacle. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the act of dyeing with madder or producing a red color.

This Greek LXX verb describes being well off or enjoying oneself. It can refer to a person’s favorable condition or to taking pleasure in life, depending on the surrounding passage. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in Job and once in Psalms. Its basic sense concerns experiencing well-being or enjoyment, rather than naming a specific object, person, or event. The exact force in either occurrence must be understood from the sentence and passage where the verb appears.

Zethom is a proper name, referring to an individual identified by this name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the person’s name itself. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles: 23:8 and 26:22. No broader lexical sense is provided for it beyond this personal name.

Zosara is a proper name, referring to someone identified by that name. The form is also rendered as “Zosara,” while its lexical definition gives “Zōsara; Zosara.” In the Greek Old Testament text, it occurs three times, all in Esther: Esther 5:10, Esther 5:14, and Esther 6:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name’s specific role in each passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore a personal name rather than a general description, action, or quality.

This Greek pronoun means “us,” referring to the speaker or writer together with at least one other person. It identifies a group that is included in an action, statement, request, or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 386 times, appearing across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact reference—whether to a small group or a wider community—comes from the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains the group that includes the speaker.

Ieththar is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:43. Because names identify individuals, its meaning here is primarily the person it names; the available information does not provide an additional definition or description. Its precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

“Ietour; Ietur” is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Greek LXX, at Genesis 25:15. Because the available information gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding context, it does not establish which person is being identified or add a broader symbolic meaning. Its ordinary meaning is therefore simply the personal name “Ietour; Ietur” within this Greek Old Testament corpus.

Ikasmōn, also rendered Ikazmon, is a proper name identifying a place or location. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 16:6. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its specific location or role cannot be explained further here. The name itself functions as a geographical designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or person.

Iouach, also written Iuakh, is a proper name in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text, in 2 Chronicles 34:8. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide a broader descriptive meaning. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person identified there.

This Greek LXX verb means to “track out” or “hunt after”—to follow a trail or pursue something deliberately. It describes active searching rather than merely noticing or waiting. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, once in Proverbs and once in Sirach. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is purposeful pursuit by following traces or seeking after something.

Iōiarib is a proper name, preserved as “Iōiarib” or “Iiariv.” It identifies a person or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:19. The available information establishes its naming function, but does not provide a further word-meaning definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain the individual’s role there.

This noun means “cleanliness; purity,” describing a condition of being clean or pure. It refers to purity as a quality or state rather than naming an action that makes something clean. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs six times, including passages in Exodus, 2 Samuel, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains cleanliness or purity.

Kariatharboxepher is a proper name, also rendered Kariatharvoksefer. It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general idea, action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Judges 1:10. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise identification in that passage cannot be explained further from the name alone. The spelling may appear in either of the two recorded renderings.

This verb means “rest.” It describes stopping work or activity and entering a state of rest. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming the rest itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears 60 times, showing a repeated scriptural use for the act of resting across many passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains ceasing from activity and resting.

This LXX verb means “bring down/against; bear down.” It describes an action that moves something downward or presses forcefully against someone or something. The word functions as a verb, so it expresses what a person or force does rather than naming an object or quality. It occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX corpus, chiefly in Old Testament books, and its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being brought down or borne against.

This Greek LXX verb means “in danger”: it describes being exposed to serious risk or peril. As a verb, it expresses a condition someone faces rather than naming the danger itself. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a focused meaning connected with situations of threat or vulnerability. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and circumstances. The word appears in Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Daniel, Jonah, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees.

This verb means “weary” or “exhaust with physical trouble.” It describes physical strain that leaves someone tired, or the act of wearing another person down through such strain. As a verb, it expresses an action or resulting condition rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, showing a focused word for bodily fatigue or exertion, rather than a broad label for every kind of difficulty.

This noun means “tassel” or “fringe,” referring to a hanging decorative strand or cluster attached to clothing or fabric. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Exodus and once in Isaiah, showing its use for an ornamental detail rather than an action or inner quality. The precise object is identified by the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

The word is the proper name “Kyrēnē,” also given as “Kirini.” It identifies a named person, place, or other entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:23. The verse text is not available in this lexical entry, so the specific referent must be determined from that passage. Its basic meaning is therefore the name itself: Kyrene, or Kirini.

Labana, also rendered Lavana, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or group in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 7:48. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about the person or group it identifies.

This Greek LXX verb means “radiate” or “shine.” It describes light being given out or appearing brightly, whether literally or as an image of brightness. As a verb, it expresses the action of shining rather than naming the light itself. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Proverbs, Isaiah, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of light.

This Greek LXX verb means to whiten—to make something white or cause it to become white. It describes a change toward whiteness rather than naming a white object. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, across four verses. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being whitened and the surrounding wording.

This is a personal name, rendered as “Maasaias” or “Maaseas.” It identifies people in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. The name occurs ten times in the LXX corpus: nine times in Old Testament books and once in Baruch. Most occurrences are in Jeremiah, with additional occurrences in 2 Chronicles and Baruch. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This adjective means “Mordecai,” identifying something connected with or belonging to Mordecai. It is a personal-name word rather than a general description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:36. Since the verse text is not provided, the word’s exact role in that sentence cannot be described further, but its basic reference is clear: Mordecai.

This Greek LXX noun refers to the “character of a,” pointing to the defining quality or distinctive impress associated with someone or something. It names a quality rather than an action. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in Psalms, so its normal sense is established across several psalm passages rather than by a single occurrence. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This adjective describes something connected with noon or occurring about noon. It identifies the time of day around midday rather than naming an object, person, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic time reference remains the same: the period of noon or midday.

This word refers to measuring or to the act or result of measurement. As a noun, it names the process of determining size, length, or quantity rather than describing the object being measured. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 7:24. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: it points to measurement itself. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being measured there, but the word’s lexical meaning remains this practical idea of measuring.

“Adulteress” refers to a woman who is unfaithful in marriage or engages in sexual relations outside the marriage covenant. It is a noun identifying the woman by that act. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs seven times across six verses, including passages in Proverbs, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Malachi. Its central meaning remains consistent: a woman guilty of adultery, whether the word is used directly or within Scripture’s broader picture of faithlessness.

Mōrad is a personal name, also given as “Morath.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:17. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the verse’s surrounding text, its particular significance in that genealogy must be understood from the passage itself. The name’s normal meaning here is therefore its function as a personal designation.

Naiman, also rendered Neman, is a proper name—the personal name of a man in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe a general quality, action, or object; it identifies a particular person. The name occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament, all within 2 Kings chapter 5, where the surrounding passage identifies the individual being discussed. Since the available word-level information does not include the verse text, the name itself supplies identification rather than a broader lexical meaning.

Naphtha is a combustible liquid substance, and this word functions as a noun naming it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 1:36. The word’s basic meaning is simply the substance itself; the available information does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain its particular use there. Its lexical meaning is explicitly given as “naphtha.”

This noun means a “small piece of wood” or “twig.” It refers to a small, slender piece broken or cut from wood, rather than to a large branch or substantial timber. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 17:12. Its basic meaning is concrete and ordinary: a small wooden stick used or gathered for a practical purpose. The surrounding verse supplies the particular situation in which it appears.

This noun means the handle of a rudder—the tiller used to steer a boat or ship. It refers to the part a person grasps to guide the vessel’s direction, rather than to the entire rudder. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:3. Its basic meaning is concrete and practical: the controlling handle by which a vessel is turned.

This adjective means “like” or “similar to,” describing something that resembles another person, thing, or quality. It identifies a comparison rather than the thing itself, helping readers recognize that two things share some likeness while remaining distinct. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 78 times, so it serves a broad descriptive function across many passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being compared and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “wild ass,” referring to a donkey-like animal living outside domestication. It names the animal itself rather than an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in Sirach. The precise force of the word in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic reference remains a wild ass.

This noun means “bone,” referring to the hard inner parts of the body. It can describe one bone or bones collectively, and it is used for the physical skeletal substance rather than for a separate abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 120 times, showing regular use across biblical descriptions of the human body. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “penalty” or “punishment”—a consequence imposed because of wrongdoing or debt. It names the corrective or judicial burden someone must bear, rather than describing the act that caused it. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Baruch 3:8; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the penalty or punishment itself.

This word means “unexpectedly” or “astonishingly.” It is an adverb, so it describes how something happens or how an action is experienced. It points to an event that occurs in a surprising way or produces wonder because it is beyond what someone anticipated. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 4:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is clear: something happens in a manner that is surprising or remarkable.

This LXX word means “thick” or “stout.” It describes something substantial in build or thickness and may function either as an adjective or a noun, depending on how it is used in a sentence. The word appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material represented here. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a description of thickness, heaviness, or stoutness.

This Greek LXX adjective means “fiftieth,” describing something that comes in position number fifty or is connected with fifty. It is an ordinal word, so it identifies a place in a sequence rather than simply naming the number itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 10 times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Leviticus, 2 Kings, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the noun or event it describes.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “noised abroad” or “much talked of.” It refers to what has become widely known and spoken about, rather than something hidden or noticed by only a few people. The word occurs once in the LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 2:22. Its exact force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is public notice and widespread conversation.

This verb means “spread out,” describing something being extended or opened across an area. It expresses the action of stretching or broadening rather than remaining gathered in one place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, including passages in 2 Samuel, Job, and Psalms. The surrounding wording determines what is being spread out in each passage, but the central idea remains extension across space.

This word means doing something faithfully—reliably, loyally, or in a trustworthy manner. As an adverb, it describes how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 16:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is steadfast and trustworthy performance.

This preposition means “before” or “ahead of,” describing something that comes earlier or stands in front of something else. It can mark position, order, or priority, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 232 times, so it is a common word for expressing what precedes another person, thing, or event. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and context.

This LXX Greek verb means “stumble” or “strike against.” It describes coming against something and being hindered, whether physically or figuratively. The word appears 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and Sirach. Its basic sense can describe losing one’s footing or encountering an obstacle that causes a person to fall or be obstructed. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means to sprinkle something on another object or person. It describes the act of applying a substance in scattered drops rather than pouring it out all at once. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus, including Leviticus 4:6 and Leviticus 8:30. Its basic meaning is precise and action-focused: something is sprinkled onto a designated recipient. The surrounding verse determines what is sprinkled and the significance of that action.

This word refers to a box-tree, a particular kind of tree. It is a noun naming the tree itself rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 41:19. The word’s basic meaning identifies a plant, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain why this tree is mentioned there and what role it has in that passage.

This noun means “remnant”: something left over after a larger part has been removed, used, or lost. It can refer to a remaining piece or portion rather than the whole. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Esther, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its exact reference may vary with the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains what is left or preserved from something greater.

This word means “furiously,” describing action carried out with intense anger or force.
